implementation_notes: Enumerator::Lazy builds chains of operations without evaluating them immediately and evaluates on demand, redefining most Enumerable methods to return another lazy enumerator; the chain only runs when an eager method such as first, to_a (force) is called (ruby-doc.org Enumerator::Lazy). The lazy chain is the pipeline - named stage blocks compose it and no pipeline object is needed - and it is the right choice for sequences, files and potentially unbounded input. For a single value, compose named stages with Proc#>> / Object#then instead.
pitfalls: The chain stays lazy only while every step is a redefined lazy method; an eager call in the middle (sort, a block-less each_slice) materialises the whole input.
to_a or force on an infinite lazy chain never returns, and first(n) on a lazy enumerator is fine only because it stops pull-side.
Blocks capture the surrounding locals and self, so pipelines built inside loops share the last iteration's bindings.

variants.name: Proc/Method composition with >> and then
variants.implementation_notes: Proc#>> and Method#>> return a composed callable: (f >> g) calls g with the result of f, forwarding the original arguments (ruby-doc.org Method#>>), while Object#then threads a value through stages one call at a time. Named methods and lambdas become the stages and the composed proc is the pipeline value, replacing the classic pipeline object for single values. Keep lazy enumeration when the payload is a sequence, because composition does not stream.
variants.code_sketch:
pipeline = method(:parse) >> ->(row) { row.normalize } >> method(:enrich)
result = pipeline.call(raw_row)
pitfalls: Method#>> was added in Ruby 2.7 (Proc#>> in 2.6); on older runtimes the composition must be a hand-written lambda.
Composed callables forward all arguments, so a stage that takes extra arguments must be wrapped or curried first.
Exceptions propagate unchanged through the composition, so per-stage error handling needs a wrapper stage rather than a rescue inside the chain.
